item.title: [International Logistics #9] Your $60,000 Shipment Flew Fine—So Why Would the Airline Only Owe You $7,000?
item.body:
> Air cargo is fast but costly, and it runs on three things: a contract document (the air waybill), standardized containers (ULDs), and an international treaty (the Montreal Convention) that caps what an airline pays if something goes wrong.

## Today's Concept

Less than 1% of world trade by weight moves by air, yet that slice accounts for roughly a third of global trade by value. That makes sense: you fly things that are light, valuable, perishable, or urgent, such as smartphones, pharmaceuticals, fresh flowers, or a replacement part for a stalled factory line.

Three building blocks keep this system running.

**1. The Air Waybill (AWB): the contract and the receipt.**
Every air shipment travels under an AWB. It shows that the airline received the goods, lays out the terms of carriage, and lists the shipper, consignee, weight, pieces, and charges. Each AWB has an 11-digit number. The first three digits are the airline's prefix (for example, 001 is American Airlines), and the remaining eight identify the shipment, so you can track it from start to finish.

One key difference from ocean shipping: **an AWB is not a document of title.** A negotiable ocean bill of lading can be sold or handed over to transfer ownership of the goods. An AWB can't. The cargo is released to the consignee named on it. Because planes arrive in hours, not weeks, nobody needs to trade the goods while they're in transit.

You will also hear about two layers of waybills:
- **Master AWB (MAWB)**: issued by the airline to a freight forwarder, often covering many customers' goods consolidated together.
- **House AWB (HAWB)**: issued by the forwarder to each individual shipper.

Most AWBs today are electronic (e-AWB) instead of paper.

**2. ULDs (Unit Load Devices): the building blocks of the cargo hold.**
Aircraft holds are curved and tightly packed, so you can't just roll in a standard 40-foot ocean container. Airlines use ULDs instead. These are aluminum pallets with nets, or contoured containers shaped to fit the fuselage. A common example is the **LD3**, a container that fits two-across in the lower deck of wide-body jets like the Boeing 777. ULDs let ground crews load hundreds of boxes as a single unit, which cuts loading time and handling damage.

**3. How air freight is priced: chargeable weight.**
Space on a plane is limited by volume as well as weight. Airlines therefore charge on whichever is greater: the actual weight, or a "volumetric weight" based on the box's size. Under the common IATA standard:

```
Volumetric weight (kg) = Length x Width x Height (cm) / 6000
```

A big box of pillows can cost far more to fly than its scale weight would suggest.

**4. The Montreal Convention (1999): who pays when things go wrong.**
This international treaty governs most international air carriage, and the U.S. is a party to it. For cargo, the main rules are:
- The airline is liable for destruction, loss, or damage during carriage, **whether or not it was at fault**. It escapes liability only for listed reasons, such as an inherent defect of the goods, defective packing by someone other than the carrier, war, or acts of public authorities (e.g., customs).
- Liability is **capped per kilogram**, measured in Special Drawing Rights (SDRs), an IMF unit based on a basket of currencies. The limit is reviewed about every five years. It is currently **26 SDRs per kg**, raised in December 2024, which comes to roughly $35 per kg depending on exchange rates.
- For cargo, that cap holds **even if the airline was seriously negligent**. The only ways around it are to declare a higher value and pay a supplementary charge when shipping, or to buy separate cargo insurance.
- Deadlines are strict: written complaints are due within **14 days** of receipt for damage and **21 days** for delay, and lawsuits must be filed within **2 years**.

## In Everyday Life

A medical-device startup in Columbus, Ohio, sells precision sensor modules to a hospital group in Germany. The order is 200 kg of modules worth **$60,000**, flown from Chicago O'Hare to Frankfurt.

Their freight forwarder consolidates the shipment with other customers' freight under one master AWB and gives the startup a house AWB. At O'Hare, the boxes go into an LD3 container on a 777.

During transit a forklift punctures the container, and half the modules are crushed. The hospital notes the damage on delivery, and the startup files a written claim within 14 days.

The airline is liable even without proof of fault. But the payout is capped:

```
200 kg x 26 SDR = 5,200 SDR ≈ about $7,000
```

That covers roughly **$7,000 of a $30,000 loss.** If the startup had declared a higher value on the AWB, or simply bought an all-risk cargo insurance policy (often a small fraction of a percent of the cargo value), it could have recovered close to the full amount. The lesson for anyone shipping high-value, lightweight goods is that the per-kilo cap is not built to protect you.

## 3-Line Summary

1. The **air waybill** is the contract and receipt for air cargo. Unlike an ocean bill of lading, it is non-negotiable, and the goods go to the named consignee.
2. **ULDs** are pallets and containers shaped to fit aircraft holds, and freight is priced on **chargeable weight**, whichever is greater of actual or volumetric weight.
3. Under the **Montreal Convention**, airlines are liable for cargo damage without proof of fault but only up to **26 SDRs/kg**. For valuable goods, declare a higher value or insure them.

## ✅ Self-Quiz

**Q1. (O/X)** An air waybill can be endorsed and sold to a third party to transfer ownership of the goods in transit, just like a negotiable ocean bill of lading.

**Q2. (Multiple choice)** A box weighs 10 kg and measures 60 cm x 50 cm x 40 cm. Using the 6,000 divisor, what is its chargeable weight?
- A) 10 kg
- B) 20 kg
- C) 30 kg
- D) 40 kg

**Q3. (Multiple choice)** Under the Montreal Convention, which is the most reliable way for a shipper of high-value cargo to recover more than the per-kg liability limit?
- A) Prove the airline was grossly negligent
- B) Declare a higher value on the AWB (paying a supplementary charge) or buy cargo insurance
- C) File the claim within 2 years instead of 14 days
- D) Ship in an LD3 container instead of on a pallet

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Air Waybill (AWB)**: A non-negotiable contract of carriage and receipt for goods shipped by air, identified by an 11-digit number.
- **Master / House AWB**: The airline-to-forwarder waybill (master) and the forwarder-to-shipper waybill (house) used in consolidated shipments.
- **ULD (Unit Load Device)**: A standardized aircraft pallet or container, such as the LD3, used to load cargo as a single unit.
- **Chargeable weight**: Whichever is greater of actual weight and volumetric weight; the figure air freight is billed on.
- **Montreal Convention (1999)**: The international treaty setting airline liability rules, including a per-kg cap (currently 26 SDRs) for cargo loss, damage, or delay.

---

*Answers: Q1 — X. An AWB is not a document of title; the goods are delivered to the consignee named on it. Q2 — B. 60 x 50 x 40 = 120,000; divided by 6,000 = 20 kg, which beats the 10 kg actual weight. Q3 — B. For cargo, the Montreal Convention limit applies even when the carrier is at fault. Only a special declaration of value (or separate insurance) gets you past it.*
